title: The prayer at forty
hookLine: at forty a person prays: inspire me to be grateful for Your favor on me and my parents (46:15)

lines: FORTY: THE BIRTHDAY PEOPLE JOKE ABOUT.
THE QUR'AN HANDS YOU A PRAYER.
cards: Forty is the birthday people joke about. Black balloons, over-the-hill cards, a friend who buys you reading glasses as a gag.

Somewhere around then, a lot of people take stock: the career, the body, the parents getting older. Surah Al-Ahqaf, the Sand Dunes, the forty-sixth surah, also marks forty. But it doesn't hand you a joke or a crisis.
It hands you a prayer, and the first thing that prayer asks for is gratitude.

teach.h: THIRTY MONTHS OF CARRYING AND WEANING.
teach.b: Verse fifteen begins with parents. It says a mother carries her child with hardship and gives birth with hardship, and that the carrying and the weaning take thirty months.
Then it follows that child to full strength, to forty years, and puts words in their mouth.
In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Arouse me that I may give thanks for the favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents." Arouse me is awzi'ni, an unusual word.

Commentators explain it as inspire me, or rouse me, or keep me constantly at it, as if gratitude were something you need help even to remember. Look at who's in the prayer. Not just me: me and my parents.
At forty, many people finally understand what their parents carried, sometimes because they're carrying it now.
The prayer goes on: that I may do good that pleases You, make my children good for me, and I turn to You in repentance. Three generations in one breath. And here's a thread from earlier this year.

teach.h: AWZI'NI: ROUSE ME TO THANK YOU.
teach.b: When Sulayman heard the ant warning her colony, in Surah An-Naml, he smiled and prayed with the same opening: rabbi awzi'ni, my Lord, rouse me to thank You for Your favor on me and my parents.

teach.h: ME AND MY PARENTS, THEN MY CHILDREN.
teach.b: A king at the height of power and an ordinary person at forty reach for the same words.
Commentators note why forty matters: the age of maturity in judgment, and the age at which, according to the biographies, revelation first came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

how: Many Muslims memorize the prayer of 46:15 and say it in their own supplications, often especially around the age of forty, and many also say Sulayman's matching words from 27:19.

o: grant me wealth to share with my parents
rouse me, keep me at it, to give thanks
forgive me for what I failed to do

games.q: the prayer at forty — tap the pairs.

s: the prayer at forty asks only for the person praying
it names parents, then good deeds, then children.
Sulayman prays with the same opening in Surah An-Naml
rabbi awzi'ni appears in 27:19 after he hears the ant.
the verse begins with a mother's hardship
it describes carrying and birth before reaching forty.

games.q: you reach forty, full strength. according to 46:15, what is the first thing the prayer asks for?
o: to be roused to give thanks.
games.why: the prayer opens by asking to be inspired to gratitude, for favor on you and your parents.

practice: Bring your parents to mind, or whoever raised you, as they are or as they were, and one thing they carried for you that you didn't see at the time.

If you pray, you can say the opening of the verse quietly: my Lord, rouse me to thank You for Your favor on me and my parents. If you don't, simply hold that one thing they carried, and say thank you in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Awzi'ni: arouse me, rouse me to give thanks, the unusual word at the heart of the prayer for me and my parents. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: my Lord, rouse me (to give thanks); in 46:15 and 27:19.

carryVoice: Your line: inspire me to thank. A king and an ordinary person at forty reach for the same words. Day five hundred seventy-six.

sources.q: My Lord! Arouse me that I may give thanks for the favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents
